posts.body_html: The marl "forms" will grow in regular peat soils like any of the other purpureas. They just take a season or two to revert to the growth pattern found in acid soils.

posts.body_html:
Thanks Rhizomatous! Several years back (maybe almost a decade ago?) we had a heat wave where it was 112F for several days, and then it dropped down to the low 100's for about 2 weeks. I didn't lose a single S. purpurea ssp. purpurea plant from the heat.

Keep in mind, there's many different genotypes of S. purpurea ssp. purpurea. The ones from New Jersey and Virginia can likely take the southern heat.

I've also heard that other people have had trouble with S. purpurea ssp. purpurea overheating (even here in California), but I haven't had any problems with them. I have some friends in Alabama who are experimenting with growing quite a few Canadian purpureas, and I'll let you know how it turns out. I've also sent several people in Florida some S. purpurea ssp. purpurea....anyone else in Florida, Georgia, or a Southern State have experience with S. purpurea ssp. purpurea?

posts.body_html:
Spring pitchers! This has to be my favorite purpurea ssp. purpurea variant: although these genotypes originate from a marl bog, the shape and look are independent of that factor: populations out there in regular, acidic bogs have the same shape and coloration. I think it just happens to be a good looking form growing in an unusual environment.

Once these new spring traps fully emerge, many of the plants are effectively double the size compared to the previous years' growth! these traps will color up as they age, they don't always start off colorful. Pics taken 4/11/20:





Here are some old historic photos from several years ago: I've had these plants since the early 2000's, so they have definitely stood the test of time in cultivation! One other reason I like them: many other populations over the decades have been difficult to keep going compared to this population, this marl bog population is more resilient for whatever reason:
